errors: The constraint att_ub says attained[j,k] <= skill[i,k] whenever x[i,j]=1, for every assigned person i. Together with att_lb (attained >= skill[i,k]), this forces every person on a project to have exactly the same level in every skill. That is not the 'highest level among assigned staff' the problem describes.

Six people must be split across four projects, so some project gets two or more people with different levels in some skill. The model is therefore infeasible, which contradicts a problem that is always feasible.

A correct upper bound on attained needs an extra binary variable per (project, skill) that selects which assigned person attains the maximum. Alternatively, the shortage can be bounded directly by the best assigned person's level.
assumptions: Projects may receive no staff; the model allows this, and the problem does not forbid it.
verdicts.reason: The upper-bound constraint makes attained the minimum and the maximum of assigned staff simultaneously, which makes the model infeasible and does not capture the max-skill definition.

errors: Constraint (3) bounds the attained level below by the SUM of assigned members' levels (sum L[p][s]*x[p,j]), not by the maximum. Combined with a <= 7, any project with two or more staff becomes infeasible, which is why the solver reports infeasible.

Even with a per-member form (a >= L*x), the direction is wrong. The attained level is the maximum of the assigned members' levels, so a must be bounded above by that maximum (needs selector binaries or a max-linearisation). A lower bound lets a be inflated and would hide shortages.
The 'each project gets at least one staff member' constraint is not stated in the problem and could change the optimum.
assumptions: The attained level is capped at 7, the largest staff skill level
verdicts.reason: The attained-skill constraint uses a sum with the wrong direction instead of a max, so the model is infeasible and does not represent the problem.

errors: Constraint 4 is applied to every assigned member i, so it forces y[j,s] <= the minimum skill of the assigned members. Combined with constraint 3 (y >= the maximum), every member of a project would need identical skill levels. The attained level is therefore not the maximum, and the model is infeasible.
Constraint 2 (each project nonempty) is not in the problem text. It is probably harmless, but it is an unsupported restriction.

A correct max linearisation would need an extra binary selector for which member attains the maximum. Alternatively, y can be left as a free lower bound, because the objective pushes it up. The model does neither.
assumptions: Every project must have at least one staff member.
verdicts.reason: The 'upper bound' constraint 4 is applied to all assigned members, which makes the attained level equal to both the maximum and the minimum. This produces the infeasible result for a problem that should be feasible.

errors: The attained-level variable a[j,k] is only bounded below (a >= skill*x) and has no upper bound or max-linking constraint. The solver can therefore inflate a[j,k] to the required level at no cost, and the shortage is always driven to 0.

The reported solution shows this: a[0,0]=9 although project 0 has only Person 0, whose Skill 0 level is 5. The best Skill 0 level anyone has is 7, so projects 0 and 2, which require 9, must have a shortage of at least 2. The true optimum is therefore greater than 0, and the reported 0.0 is spurious.
assumptions: Each project is required to have at least one staff member. The text does not state this.
verdicts.reason: The attained skill level is not tied to the maximum of the assigned staff's levels, so the model reports zero shortage when the true minimax shortage is at least 2.

errors: The max-chain constraint `req - skill*(x+y) <= w` is written for every person and project, including people not assigned to that project. For an unassigned person x=0 and y=0, so it forces w >= req. The reported objective of 9 is simply the largest requirement, not a real shortage.

The attained level is never modelled as the maximum over the assigned staff. The skill is multiplied by (x+y), so a person with y=1 counts double, and people outside the project still impose constraints.
The constraint x_implies_y reduces to x <= 1, which is trivial. y is therefore not tied to the highest-skilled assigned person, so it does not select the maximum.
The constraint projstaffed (each project needs at least one person) is not in the problem text. It is probably harmless here, since six people can cover four projects, but it is unsupported.
The shortage is not floored at 0. The problem defines shortage as required minus attained, so the intended model should use a nonnegative shortage.
verdicts.reason: The max-skill logic is broken: every unassigned person forces w >= req, so the optimum of 9 is an artifact of the model and the true minimax shortage is far smaller.

errors: The attained level v[j,s] is only bounded below by A[p][s]*x[p,j], so it is not forced to equal the maximum skill of the assigned staff. The shortage constraint T >= R - v pushes v up, so v rises to its upper bound of 7 even where no assigned person has that level. The reported solution shows this: project 1 holds persons 1, 3 and 4, who all have skill 1 at level 5, yet v[1,1]=7. The model therefore understates every shortage and returns T=2, the bound from the maximum requirement minus 7.

The true optimum is at least 4. Only person 5 has skill 1 at level 7, and every other person has level 5. At most one project can contain person 5, so at least two of projects 0, 2 and 3 lack him. Their skill-1 shortages are at least 4 for project 0 or 2 and 3 for project 3, so the maximum shortage is at least 4, not 2.
assumptions: The added constraint that every project gets at least one person is not in the text, but it does not change the optimum, because an empty project would have a shortage of at least 7.
verdicts.reason: The attained level is not tied to the maximum of the assigned staff's skills and can be inflated for free, so the reported objective of 2 understates the true minimax shortage of at least 4.

errors: The attained level y[j,k] is only bounded below by the assigned staff's skills. Nothing bounds it above, so the optimizer can set y to the full requirement for every project and skill, and the shortage is then 0 regardless of who is assigned.

In the reported solution all six staff are on project 0, yet y[1,*], y[2,*] and y[3,*] equal the requirements for projects with no staff. This violates the rule that attained level is the highest level among the staff assigned to that project.

The true optimum is strictly positive. The highest level any person has in skills 0, 1 and 2 is 7, so projects 0 and 2, which need 9 in skills 0 and 1, always have a shortage of at least 2. The reported objective of 0 is therefore wrong.
assumptions: Shortage is taken as required minus attained without clipping at 0, which is harmless here.
verdicts.reason: y has no upper-bounding constraint tying it to the maximum of the assigned staff's skills, so it is inflated to the requirements and the model returns a false objective of 0 when the true optimum is at least 2.
